title: Addition Polymers
subtitle: The double bond opens and the chain grows
subject: Chemistry
syllabusDotPoints: model and compare the structure, properties and uses of addition polymers of ethylene and related monomers
inquiryQuestion: What are the properties and uses of polymers?
lessonIntent: Students can describe addition polymerisation, draw repeat units and monomers, and explain how chain branching and side groups control polymer properties.
examSkill: Convert between monomer and repeat unit with correct notation, and link structure such as branching or a C-F sheath to physical properties and uses.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is HSC Chemistry. Today, addition polymers, where one double bond builds a chain. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: One gas, a thousand products
scenes.body: Ethene is a colourless gas that drifts away in seconds. Join thousands of them, with no atoms added, and you get polyethylene: from cling film to milk crates.
scenes.callout: What happens to the C=C double bond when the monomers join up?
scenes.caption: Thousands of ethene molecules link into polyethylene with no atoms lost.

voiceover.text: OK, here's something to sit with. Ethene is a colourless gas, a single small molecule that just drifts away. But link thousands of ethene molecules together, end to end, with no atoms added and none removed, and you get polyethylene, one of the most useful materials on Earth. Depending on how the chains are arranged, the same starting molecule gives you cling film thin enough to see through, or a milk crate tough enough to stand on. Today you'll learn how that linking happens, and the central question is this. What happens to the carbon-carbon double bond when the monomers join? Does it stay, or does it disappear? The answer shapes everything about the polymer.

scenes.heading: The pi bond opens
scenes.body: In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond of each monomer opens, and the freed electrons form new single bonds linking the monomers into a chain.

bullets.text: In these vinyl examples, each monomer contains a C=C.
The pi bond opens; each carbon forms a new single bond to the next monomer.
No atoms are added or removed, so there is no by-product.
For these monoalkene examples, the polymer backbone has single bonds.

scenes.secondary: Ethene gives the repeat unit shown as a CH2-CH2 unit in brackets with subscript n.
scenes.callout: Addition: the double bond opens, no by-product forms.
scenes.caption: Addition polymerisation: the C=C opens to single bonds, with no by-product.

voiceover.text: Let's get the mechanism clear, because it's the heart of the lesson. Addition polymerisation needs monomers that contain a carbon-carbon double bond, like ethene. That double bond is made of two parts, a strong sigma bond and a weaker pi bond. In the reaction, the pi bond of each monomer opens up, and the electrons that were in it form new single bonds to the neighbouring monomers. Link enough of them and you have a long chain. The crucial feature is that no atoms are added and none are removed. Every atom of every monomer ends up in the polymer, so there is no by-product at all. And notice what's left. In the polymer chain, the double bonds are gone. The repeat unit has only single bonds. For these monoalkene examples, leaving that backbone double bond is an error. Diene addition polymers are different: polybutadiene can retain carbon-carbon double bonds.

props.title: The π bond opens, the chain grows

scenes.heading: Repeat unit notation

bullets.text: Draw two backbone carbons with single bonds, inside square brackets.
Add open bonds extending from both bracket ends for chain continuation.
Write subscript n outside the closing bracket.
To find the monomer, put the C=C back and remove the chain-continuation bonds.

scenes.callout: Brackets, open bonds, and subscript n: all three are required.
scenes.caption: Repeat unit notation: square brackets, open bonds, and subscript n.

voiceover.text: Now the notation, because the exam is strict about it. To draw a repeat unit, you take the two backbone carbons, now joined by a single bond, and you write them inside square brackets. Then you add open bonds, short lines extending out from both ends of the bracket, to show that the chain continues in both directions. And finally you write a subscript n just outside the closing bracket, meaning the unit repeats many times. All three of those are required. Brackets, open bonds, and the n. Leave any one out and it's marked as incomplete. And the reverse skill is just as common. To find the monomer from a repeat unit, you put the carbon-carbon double bond back between the two backbone carbons, remove the chain-continuation bonds and check each carbon has four bonds; do not add extra hydrogens. That regenerates the original alkene.

scenes.heading: Branching and side groups set properties
scenes.body: Polyethylene comes in two forms from the same monomer. The difference is chain branching, which changes how closely the chains pack.

bullets.text: HDPE: linear chains pack closely, so strong dispersion forces, rigid, denser.
LDPE: branched chains pack poorly, so weaker forces, flexible, less dense.
Side groups matter too: polar C-Cl bonds affect PVC’s stiffness and glass transition.
PTFE's strong C-F bonds make it inert and non-stick.

scenes.callout: Closer packing means stronger dispersion forces, so a rigid, denser polymer.
scenes.caption: Linear HDPE packs closely and is rigid; branched LDPE packs loosely and bends.

voiceover.text: Now properties, and here's the elegant part. Polyethylene comes in two very different forms, even though both are made from the exact same monomer, ethene. The difference is chain branching. High-density polyethylene, HDPE, has linear, unbranched chains that pack closely together. Close packing means more contact area, so stronger dispersion forces, which makes HDPE rigid, denser, and higher melting, good for milk crates and pipes. Low-density polyethylene, LDPE, has branched chains that can't pack closely, so the dispersion forces are weaker and the material is flexible and less dense, perfect for cling film and bags. Side groups change things too. In PVC, the polar carbon-chlorine bonds add dipole forces and raise the melting point. And in PTFE, the very strong carbon-fluorine bonds make it chemically inert and non-stick. Structure sets the properties, every time.

scenes.heading: Thermoplastic, and why it persists
scenes.body: Most addition polymers are thermoplastics, and their unreactive carbon backbone is exactly why they linger in the environment.

bullets.text: Thermoplastics soften and remould on heating; chains are held by IMFs only.
They can often be remoulded; practical recycling depends on material, additives and facilities.
The C-C backbone is non-polar and inert, so ordinary microbial degradation is usually very slow.
They fragment by UV and abrasion into persistent microplastics.

scenes.callout: An inert C-C backbone means recyclable, but non-biodegradable.
scenes.caption: Addition polymers are recyclable thermoplastics but non-biodegradable.

voiceover.text: Two more ideas that round out the topic, one practical, one environmental. Most addition polymers are thermoplastics, which means they soften and can be remoulded when heated, then harden again on cooling. That's because the chains are held together only by intermolecular forces, which loosen with heat and reform on cooling. The upshot is that thermoplastics can often be remoulded; practical recycling depends on additives and available facilities. But the same carbon backbone that makes them so useful is also why they're an environmental problem. The carbon-carbon backbone is non-polar and chemically inert, so ordinary microbial degradation of these polymers is generally very slow. Instead of biodegrading, the plastic slowly fragments under ultraviolet light and physical abrasion into ever smaller pieces, the microplastics now found everywhere from deep ocean sediment to human blood. Practical recycling depends on material and facilities; ordinary biodegradation is usually very slow.

scenes.heading: Monomer and repeat unit of PVC
scenes.question: Draw the chloroethene repeat unit and explain how polarity and plasticisers influence PVC’s properties.
scenes.coachNote: Open the C=C to single bonds, bracket one unit with open bonds and subscript n, then reason from intermolecular forces.
steps: Convert CH₂=CHCl to the repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl–, inside brackets with continuation bonds and n.
Do not add extra H atoms; check carbon valency.
Polar C–Cl bonds influence interchain interactions.
Packing, crystallinity and additives also determine behaviour.
Plasticisers make PVC more flexible; avoid a universal PVC-versus-PE melting-point claim.
scenes.caption: Repeat-unit valency and contextual structure–property reasoning.

voiceover.text: Chloroethene is C H two double bond C H Cl. Its repeat unit is C H two joined by a single bond to C H Cl, with brackets, chain-continuation bonds and n. No extra hydrogen atoms are added. Now compare structure and properties. PVC has polar carbon-chlorine bonds that influence interactions between chains, while polyethylene is non-polar. But packing, crystallinity, branching and plasticisers also matter. Unplasticised PVC is relatively rigid; plasticisers can make it flexible. Do not infer a universal higher melting point from polarity alone. Ordinary PVC softens through its glass transition and can degrade on heating, whereas polyethylene has a crystalline melting transition.

scenes.heading: "The double bond stays in the polymer"
scenes.body: Students draw the repeat unit of an addition polymer with the C=C still present. It is not there.
scenes.secondary: The pi bond of the C=C is consumed to form the new single bonds that link the monomers. The monoalkene examples have a single-bonded backbone. Diene addition polymers, such as polybutadiene, can retain C=C bonds.
scenes.callout: For these monoalkene examples, the backbone C=C is consumed; diene polymers can retain C=C.
scenes.mistakeTag: Monoalkene rule; dienes can retain C=C
scenes.caption: The C=C is consumed in polymerisation; the repeat unit has only single bonds.

voiceover.text: Here's the most common addition-polymer mistake. Students draw the repeat unit and leave the carbon-carbon double bond sitting inside it, as if the monomer just got copied. But think about what the reaction actually does. The whole point of addition polymerisation is that the pi bond of the double bond opens and its electrons are used to form the new single bonds that join the monomers into a chain. So that double bond is consumed. It's gone. The monoalkene examples have a single-bonded backbone; diene polymers can retain unsaturation. A quick self-check you can always apply. For a monoalkene such as ethene, the backbone double bond is consumed. This rule is not universal: polybutadiene formed from a diene can retain a double bond. Draw the monomer with the double bond, draw these monoalkene polymer backbones with single bonds; do not apply that rule to every diene polymer. Keep those two pictures separate.

scenes.heading: Your turn
scenes.question: Identify the monomer of the polymer with repeat unit shown as a CH2-CH(CH3) unit, name it, and state the polymerisation type.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause and put the double bond back before the answer plays.
answerSteps: The repeat unit has two backbone carbons: a CH2 and a CH bearing a CH3 group.
Put the C=C back between the two backbone carbons.
Remove chain-continuation bonds and restore C=C; check valency without adding extra hydrogens.
The polymer is polypropylene, made by addition polymerisation, with no by-product.
scenes.caption: Repeat unit CH2-CH(CH3) comes from propene by addition polymerisation.

voiceover.text: Your turn. You're given a polymer whose repeat unit is a C-H-2 group joined to a C-H carrying a methyl group. Identify the monomer, name it, and state the type of polymerisation. Pause now, and remember to put the double bond back. Let's check. The repeat unit has two backbone carbons, one is a C-H-2, the other is a C-H bearing a methyl side group. To get the monomer, you reinsert the carbon-carbon double bond between those two backbone carbons, remove the chain continuation bonds and restore the double bond, then check valency without adding extra hydrogen. That gives you C-H-2 double bond C-H-C-H-3, which is propene. So the polymer is polypropylene, and it's made by addition polymerisation, with no by-product, because the double bond simply opened to link the monomers. Reverse the mechanism and the monomer falls out.

scenes.heading: Summary
scenes.finalPrompt: Monoalkene polymer: consume the backbone C=C; diene polymers can retain unsaturation.
points: Addition polymerisation: the C=C of each monomer opens to link them, with no by-product.
For these monoalkene examples, the backbone has single bonds; include brackets, continuation bonds and n.
HDPE has linear chains and packs closely; LDPE is branched, so it is flexible and less dense.
Side groups change properties: polar C-Cl in PVC, inert C-F in PTFE.
Many common vinyl polymers are thermoplastics; recycling depends on material and facilities, and crosslinking changes behaviour.
scenes.caption: The C=C opens, the monoalkene backbone is single-bonded; structure influences properties.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five takeaways. First, addition polymerisation works by opening the carbon-carbon double bond of each monomer to link them, and crucially, no by-product is formed. Second, the repeat unit has only single bonds, and the notation needs all three of brackets, open bonds, and a subscript n. Third, structure controls properties. Linear HDPE packs closely and is rigid and dense, while branched LDPE packs loosely and is flexible and less dense, both from the same ethene monomer. Fourth, side groups matter too, with polar carbon-chlorine bonds influencing PVC’s stiffness and glass transition; ordinary PVC softens and can degrade rather than showing a simple clean melting point and strong carbon-fluorine bonds making PTFE inert and non-stick. And fifth, many common vinyl polymers resist biodegradation. Thermoplastic behaviour and recyclability depend on structure, additives and available processes. So for the monoalkene examples here, the double bond opens, no by-product forms, and the backbone is all single bonds. See you next lesson.
